doc.title: John Fedchock interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 28, 2015

title: How he plans a big band composition
summary: He needs the themes and form first, maps ahead in his head, and avoids predictability, as in a blues with an extended phrase.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: For original compositions for big band, do you need to have the whole song first? Like lead sheet, melody and chords?

If I’m writing for the big band I guess it depends on the type of tune it is, but in a general sense yes. I need to have an idea of how it starts and how it ends as far as the initial themes. You know, how I develop them over the course of the arrangement, that remains to be seen what’s going to happen. But the general sense, the ebb and flow of the melody and the form of the tune, I kind of have got to have that to start with. Actually I recently just started writing some things that I just start writing and see where it goes, but because I don’t have that visual of the paper and pencil where I can like lay out four or five score pages and actually kind of visualize it, it’s hard to do page by page. So I’m still trying to work on it and I’m getting over that hurdle.

How do you deal with the idea that introduction, melody, you have a bridge, maybe go back — it’s almost like A-A-B-A, whatever — and you do that much and you get to this point and then what? Do you have things in mind where you can go other than just okay tenor solo?

Yeah. I usually try to do something where it’s not predictable kind of in 8-bar phrases or whatever. And usually I kind of plan in my head before I start writing. And once I have the themes and the general sense of what the tune is — I kind of map it out in my head before I go to paper or to the computer, just as to what the general idea is and what’s going to happen next. Like after the tune itself is over is there going to be some type of sendoff into a solo or is it going to be an ensemble section that develops some of the themes, or is there going to be just some kind of brief interlude, am I going to stretch the form, am I going to keep it squared off. You know, all those types of things. And usually because I’ve written so many other things in my life, always when I get to that point and I think of something it’s usually I’m trying to think of something I haven’t done before. Now obviously you’re going to do similar things, people have their way of writing. But I always try to approach it in a way that lets — if it’s this kind of tune or I’ve written this kind of tune before and when it gets to this part of this kind of tune I don’t want to do what I did on this or this. So I try to find new ways to do it, either by — well on the new album I have a blues. It’s a 12-bar blues. And after the tune there is a little bit of a sendoff into a solo, but rather — and then staying within the standard form of the blues I
alter one of the phrases to be extra long. So it’s just enough to kind of throw you off. You’re expecting the four chord to come in bar five but it comes in bar six. Or something like that.
